Hook: In 1932 the United States was three years into the Great Depression, and nobody could say how much the country's income had fallen. There were indexes: industrial production had halved since 1929. There were prices of shares, freight loadings, scattered surveys. But there was no total. In 1932 a senator from Wisconsin, Robert La Follette, pushed through a resolution asking the Department of Commerce for the national income of the last three years. The work went to a young economist at the National Bureau of Economic Research, Simon Kuznets, who had been born in Pinsk, in what is now Belarus, and had come to America in 1922. On the fourth of January 1934, the report went to the Senate. It ran to nearly two hundred and seventy pages, and it was the first official estimate of the national income of the United States.

Its first table answered the senator's question. In 1929 the American economy produced an income of 83 billion dollars. By 1932 it produced 39 billion: a fall of more than half in three years. The income actually paid out to people, in wages, salaries, dividends, interest and rent, fell less, by 40 percent. The gap was business as a whole making a loss. In 1932, firms paid out nine and a half billion dollars more than they earned.

The second table showed who had lost it. Set each kind of income in 1929 at one hundred percent, and look at 1932. Interest was still being paid almost in full: 96.7 percent of what it had been. People who had lent money, to companies and to governments, were still collecting. Dividends had fallen to 43 percent. And the wages paid in mining, manufacturing, construction and the railways, the industries where the report could count wage earners separately, had fallen to 40 percent: down by six tenths, as factories closed and the people still working took cuts. Before 1934, nobody could have drawn this picture.

And on page seven, before any of the numbers, the report warned its readers what they could not do with them. The welfare of a nation, it said, can scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income. The measure left out work that is never sold, and the report's example was the work of housewives. It said nothing about who received the income. And it counted the pay for a job, but not how hard or how unpleasant the job was. The number became the most watched statistic in the world, and the warning is still worth reading.

This part is about one question: how do you put a number on an economy? What exactly do you add up, when every sale is also somebody's purchase? How do you compare one year with the next, when prices have changed? How do you compare two countries, when a dollar buys different things in each? And what does the number leave out?
Economics, Built. Part three: the measure.

Part two opened the first two pipes of the Tableau, spending and goods, and found the price where they meet. This part opens no new pipes. It puts a meter on every one. The national accounts are the meter readings of a whole economy: what flows from households to firms, from firms to the government, to the rest of the world, in a year. Kuznets read the first meters by hand. We'll build the meters for the Island, read them for the United States, and ask, at every step, what they cannot see.

Part three: the measure. We'll keep the Island's accounts three ways, by what it produces, by what it spends and by what it earns, and see why the three must agree. We'll ask what the number leaves out. We'll compare one year with the next, which turns out to depend on whose basket of goods you price, and you'll play with two baskets yourself. We'll compare countries, measure unemployment with a survey, and ask who gets the income. And we'll finish with Leontief's table of who buys from whom, the revisions that rewrite history, and the attempts to measure what GDP does not.
ThreeWays: On the Island, the books are kept by Dara. There are four businesses: the fishing company, the coconut grove, the boatyard and the ferry. In a year they sold 380 dollars' worth of fish, 300 of coconuts and coconut products, 185 of boats and repairs, and 110 of passages and freight. Some of those sales were to each other. The grove sold fibre to the fishing company for its nets, the boatyard repaired the fishing boats and the ferry, and the ferry carried everyone's goods. Add up all the sales and you get 975 dollars. But that number counts some things twice. The coconut fibre is counted once when the grove sells it, and again inside the price of the fish caught with the nets made from it. A total of sales grows every time one firm buys from another, even if nothing more is made.

The fix is to count, for each business, only what it added. Start with each one's sales. Take away everything it bought and used up to make them: the fibre, the repairs, the freight, and the nets, nails and fuel it imported. What is left is the business's value added, the value it created itself. The fishing company sold 380 dollars of fish with 105 dollars of inputs, and so added 275. Add the four: 275, 290, 110 and 65 make 740 dollars. That is the Island's gross domestic product, measured by output: the value of everything produced on the Island in the year, with each thing counted once.

Now count from the other end: who bought what was produced, for their own use and not to make something else. Households bought 610 dollars of fish, coconuts, passages and cloth. That's consumption. Crusoe's boatyard built two new boats for the fishing company: 120 dollars of investment, goods bought to produce more in later years. The island council bought 30, and visiting ships bought 120 of fish and coconuts: exports. That adds up to 880, which is too much, because some of what was bought wasn't made on the Island. The cloth was imported, and so were the nets, nails and fuel used up inside the fish and the boats. Take away the imports, 140, and you're back at 740. Consumption plus investment plus government plus exports minus imports: GDP measured by spending, the most famous identity in macroeconomics.

The third way is Petty's: count the incomes. Every dollar a business adds has to go to somebody. Most of it, 450 dollars, went to the people who did the work, as wages. 250 was left for the owners, as profit. And 40 went to the council, as taxes on production. 450 plus 250 plus 40 is 740 again. This isn't a coincidence, and it isn't a theory. It's bookkeeping. Profit is defined as what is left after everyone else is paid, so value added and the incomes it pays must be equal. And every sale is somebody's purchase, so output and spending must be equal too. Three ways of reading the same transactions give one number.

Here are the three ways in one picture. In the middle, the value added by each business. On the left, where it went: each business's wages, profits and taxes flow out to the three kinds of income. On the right, what it was for: the fish, coconuts, boats and passages end up in households' consumption, in investment, with the council, and on the visiting ships, once the imported parts are taken out. Every column is 740 dollars tall. This is what economists mean by the circular flow: the same dollars, earned, produced and spent.

The identities have a famous consequence. Call what the Island earned but didn't spend on consumption or on the council its national saving: 740, minus 610, minus 30, is 100 dollars. Put that together with the spending identity, and saving must equal investment plus net exports. The Island saved 100 and invested 120, and the difference, 20, is exactly its trade deficit. A country that invests more than it saves must borrow the difference from the rest of the world, whatever its trade policy. We'll lean on that identity when we open the trade and capital pipes, in Parts 34 to 36.

The United States keeps exactly these books, on a larger scale. In 2025, American households spent 20.9 trillion dollars on consumption, businesses and home builders invested 5.6 trillion dollars, governments, federal, state and local, bought 5.4 trillion dollars, and foreigners bought 3.3 trillion dollars of American exports. Take away 4.3 trillion dollars of imports, and GDP was 30.86 trillion dollars. Measured by income, it was 30.91 trillion dollars. In real data the two sides don't quite agree, because they're built from different sources: spending from sales and surveys of businesses, income from tax records and payrolls. The gap, 46 billion dollars this year, is published under its honest name: the statistical discrepancy.

Kept every year since 1929, the spending side tells the century's story. Consumption is usually about two thirds of the American economy, and investment the swingiest part, collapsing in the Depression. In 1944, at the height of the war, government bought 48 percent of everything the country produced. That's the number Keynes, Meade and Stone needed: how much a country can turn to war, and what must give way. And since the 1970s, net exports have been mostly below zero: by the identity we just saw, America has invested more than it saved, and borrowed the rest.
InOut: Chapter three. What is in, and what is left out.

GDP measures production, but not all of it. Statisticians draw a line, the production boundary, and count what falls inside. Inside is everything sold at a price. Government services are inside too, valued at what they cost to provide, because a school or a court has no price. So is food a farmer grows and eats herself. And so is something odd: the rent that people who own their homes would pay if they rented them. Kuznets left that out in 1934, about two point seven billion dollars in 1930. Today it's counted, so that a country's GDP doesn't change just because its people buy the homes they used to rent. Outside the line is most of the work done at home: cooking, cleaning, looking after children. So is volunteering, and leisure, and most of the value of things given away free online. And a fishery fished out or a river polluted subtracts nothing at all. GDP counts the catch, not the stock it came from.

On the Island we can count what the books leave out, because we planted it. In the year, the islanders spent hours cooking and cleaning, looking after children, working Crusoe's garden and mending nets at home. Valued at what the same hours would earn at the fishing company, that work was worth 230 dollars: 31 percent of the Island's GDP, and none of it in the accounts. It leads to a famous oddity. If Bo pays Ana to cook for his family, her wages are income and the meals are production, and GDP goes up. If they marry and she cooks the same meals for nothing, GDP goes down, though nobody eats any less.

This isn't only an Island story. In 2012 economists at the Bureau of Economic Analysis built a satellite account for the United States, valuing the hours people spend on home production. Counting it would have made GDP 39 percent larger in 1965, and 26 percent larger in 2010. The share fell because people spent less time on it, 27 hours a week on average in 1965 and 22 in 2010, as more women took paid work. So part of the growth in measured GDP over those decades was work that moved from the home, where it wasn't counted, to the market, where it was. Counted properly, growth was a little slower: 6.7 percent a year in current dollars instead of 6.9.

Two more gaps are large. In much of the world most work is informal: street trade, small farms, jobs with no contract and no tax records. The International Labour Organization estimated in 2018 that more than 61 percent of the world's workers, about two billion people, worked informally, and in Africa almost 86 percent. The accounting rules ask countries to estimate this work, but it's the part they measure worst. And at the other end, the digital economy gives much away. A search engine, a map or a social network costs its users nothing, so it adds almost nothing to GDP beyond the advertising it sells. Erik Brynjolfsson and his colleagues ran large online experiments, asking people what they would need to be paid to give such things up. The median user wanted about 48 dollars to go without Facebook for a month. None of this makes GDP wrong. It measures market production, carefully and consistently, and it stops at the edge of the market, as Kuznets said it would.
Real: Chapter four. Real and nominal: whose basket?

Here is American GDP every year since 1929, measured two ways. In white, in the dollars of each year: what the books add up to. From 1929 to 2025 it grew 295 times over. In gold, in the dollars of a single year, 2017: it grew 20 times. The gap between them is prices. A dollar of 2025 buys much less than a dollar of 1929, and most of the growth in the white line is inflation: 6.1 percent a year in current dollars, 3.2 percent a year in real terms. Even the Depression looks different. In current dollars GDP fell 45 percent between 1929 and 1933. Prices fell too, so the real fall, the fall in what was actually produced, was 26 percent: still the worst in the country's history.

Kuznets did the same thing in 1934. To turn a nominal number into a real one, divide by an index of prices. Income paid out fell from 81 billion dollars to 49. But the Bureau of Labor Statistics' cost-of-living index fell too, by about a fifth. So in dollars of 1929, income paid out fell from 81 billion to 61: by 25 percent, not 40. Everything rests on the price index. And a price index hides a question with no single answer.

To measure the price level, you price a basket of goods in two years and compare. In 1871 a German economist, Étienne Laspeyres, proposed the obvious basket: what people bought in the first year. Price it at the old prices and at the new, and divide. Three years later Hermann Paasche proposed the other obvious basket: what people buy now. If people bought the same things in both years, the two would agree. But they don't, and the reason is the subject of Part two: when the price of something rises, people buy less of it. So the old basket gives too much weight to the goods that got dearer, and the new basket too little. Which one is right? Before I tell you, you'll work it out yourself.
PlayIt: Chapter five. Play it: two baskets.

Bo runs the ferry, and his household lives on fish and coconuts. He spends a hundred dollars a week, and he likes to split it evenly: half on fish, half on coconuts. In a calm year fish cost two dollars and coconuts one, so Bo buys 25 fish and 50 coconuts. Then comes a stormy year. The boats stay in more often, and fish doubles to four dollars. Coconuts stay at one. Bo still spends half on each, so now he buys twelve and a half fish and the same 50 coconuts. Here's your question. How much did Bo's cost of living rise? How much more money would he need in the stormy year to be exactly as well off as in the calm one? A hundred percent, because fish doubled? Fifty? Forty-one? Thirty-three? Pause, and pick one.

Three answers have names. Laspeyres's index prices the calm-year basket, 25 fish and 50 coconuts. It cost a hundred dollars in the calm year and costs a hundred and fifty in the stormy one: up 50 percent. That's answer B. Paasche's index prices the stormy-year basket, twelve and a half fish and 50 coconuts. It costs a hundred now and would have cost seventy-five before: up a third. That's D. In 1922 the American economist Irving Fisher, after comparing well over a hundred formulas, recommended the geometric mean of the two, which he called ideal. Here it's the square root of two: up 41.4 percent. Answer C. Three formulas, three answers, from the same prices. Which is right?

On the Island we can check, because Bo's tastes are planted, so we know exactly what makes him better or worse off. Here are fish across and coconuts up. In the calm year, a hundred dollars lets Bo reach any point on this line, and he chooses 25 fish and 50 coconuts. This green curve is every basket that leaves him exactly as well off as that. In the stormy year his hundred dollars buys less fish, and the best he can do lies on a lower curve. Laspeyres says: give him fifty percent more. With a hundred and fifty dollars he could buy his old basket. But he wouldn't: with fish dear and coconuts cheap, he swaps some fish for coconuts and ends up above the green curve, better off than before. Laspeyres overpays him. The least that puts him back on the green curve is 141 dollars 42: forty-one point four percent more. Answer C. Laspeyres overstates the rise because it ignores that Bo can switch. Paasche understates it because it pretends switching cost him nothing. Fisher's mean lands between them. For tastes like Bo's it is exact, and for most others it comes very close: economists call indexes like it superlative.

One more twist. Baskets go out of date, so statistical agencies chain their indexes: they compare each period with the one before, with up-to-date baskets, and multiply the links together. Let the storms come and go for twelve seasons, so that at the end prices are exactly where they started. A good index should end where it began, at one. Chained Laspeyres ends at 2.03: it says prices doubled, though nothing has changed. Each storm it overstates the rise, and each calm it understates the fall. Chained Paasche drifts the other way, to 0.49. Chained Fisher ends at exactly one. This is called chain drift, and it's why the United States has measured real GDP with chained Fisher indexes since 1996: the chained 2017 dollars on the gold line a minute ago.
CPI: Chapter six. The consumer price index.

The most watched price index in America is the consumer price index, made by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It starts with a basket: what households spend their money on, from a survey of their spending. Every month, the bureau's staff record prices in 75 urban areas, in about 23,000 shops and 6,000 homes for rents. And it combines them, each price weighted by its share of the basket. Since 2023 the weights have been updated every year. A great deal is tied to this number. Social Security payments rise each year with one version of it, the index for wage earners. Federal tax brackets move with another, the chained index. So do many wage contracts, rents and the government's inflation-protected bonds. If it's wrong by a point a year, a great deal of money moves for no reason.

In 1995 the Senate Finance Committee asked five economists, led by Michael Boskin of Stanford, how far the index was from a true cost of living. Their report, in December 1996, said it overstated inflation by about 1.1 percentage points a year, plausibly anywhere from 0.8 to 1.6. They added it up by source. About 0.15 came from substitution between goods, Bo's problem: a fixed basket ignores that people switch from beef to chicken when beef gets dear. A quarter of a point came from substitution within a good, between brands and varieties. A tenth came from new kinds of shop: when a discount store opens, the index treated its lower prices as lower quality, not as cheaper goods. And the largest part, 0.6, came from new products and better quality. A computer that costs the same as last year's but is twice as fast is really cheaper, and the index mostly didn't see it. The commission also put a price on the bias. Left alone, it would add about a trillion dollars to the federal debt over twelve years, through indexed benefits and tax brackets.

How do you see quality? The usual tool is a hedonic regression, and the Island has a test case. Here are the boats Crusoe's yard sold last year, by length and price. And here are this year's. They're longer: fishers want bigger boats. The average price rose 25 percent. Is that inflation? Mostly not: this year's buyers got more boat. So fit the price to the length in both years at once, and let the regression find how much more a boat of the same length costs this year. The answer: 2.5 percent. The rest of the rise was quality. The truth we planted was three percent, inside the interval. Statistical agencies do this for computers, phones, clothing and housing, and it's one reason the index's bias has shrunk since 1996.

The bureau changed its methods after the report. It began averaging prices within each item with a geometric mean, which allows for switching between brands, and widened its quality adjustments. And it started a second index, the chained CPI, which uses a superlative formula and so allows for switching between goods, Bo's switch. Here they are since December 1999, both starting at one hundred. The official index has doubled. The chained one has risen less: 2.62 percent a year against 2.36. That gap, about a quarter of a point every year for 27 years, is substitution bias, measured directly. The Fed targets another index, for personal consumption expenditures, which is chained too and covers more of what households consume. It has risen 0.35 points a year less than the CPI. Later audits put the official index's remaining bias at about 0.85 points a year: smaller than in 1996, and not zero. We'll put the estimates on a dial in chapter thirteen.
Countries: To compare countries you need one unit, and the obvious one is the dollar. Convert each country's GDP at the market exchange rate, and in 2024 the United States produced 29.3 trillion dollars, China 18.7 trillion and India 3.8. But a dollar changed into rupees buys far more in Delhi than in Dallas. A haircut, a bus ride or a restaurant meal costs much less there, because those are services that can't be shipped across borders, and they're cheap where wages are low. The exchange rate is set by the things that are traded, oil and machines and money. So converting at the exchange rate undercounts what poor countries actually produce.

The fix is to price the same things everywhere. The World Bank's International Comparison Program collects prices for one long list of goods and services in nearly every country, and from them works out purchasing power parities: how many rupees, or yuan, buy what a dollar buys in America. Divide a country's GDP at market rates by its GDP at those parities and you get its price level. Here is every country with more than a million people, by income and price level, each dot sized by population. The pattern is one of the most reliable in economics: richer countries are dearer. In 2024 prices in Switzerland were eleven percent above America's, China's were about half, and India's about a quarter. Bela Balassa and Paul Samuelson explained it in 1964. Rich countries are rich mostly because their factories and offices are productive, and that pushes up wages for everyone, barbers included, though a haircut takes as long in Zurich as in Delhi.

Now redraw the world. Each circle is a country, placed near its capital, with its area proportional to its GDP converted at market exchange rates. The United States is the largest, at twenty-nine trillion dollars, and China second. Now convert at purchasing power parity instead, keeping America the same size, since by definition a dollar buys a dollar's worth there. China becomes the largest economy in the world, at 38 trillion. India quadruples, to 15.6 trillion, and the poorer half of the world swells. The world's GDP goes from about 111 trillion dollars to about 197. Which is right? Both, for different questions. To pay for imports, or a foreign debt, the exchange rate is what counts. To compare how much people can eat, wear and live in, use purchasing power.

Purchasing power parities are estimates, and estimates get revised. In late 2007 the World Bank published a new round of price comparisons for 2005, the first full round in which China took part. Angus Deaton and Alan Heston later took it apart. China's economy, measured at parity, was revised to 40 percent smaller than before, and India's to 36 percent smaller. Prices there were higher than the older guesses had assumed. In China they had been collected only in and around eleven cities, where prices are higher than in the countryside, so the revision may have gone too far. Nothing in either economy had changed. Only the measure had. If you want a rougher check, The Economist has published its Big Mac index since 1986: purchasing power parity, with a basket of one burger.
Unemployment: Chapter eight. Unemployment is a survey.

The unemployment rate isn't counted from claims for benefits. It comes from a survey. Every month the Census Bureau interviews about sixty thousand American households for the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and sorts every adult with two questions. Last week, did you do any work for pay, even an hour? If yes, you're employed. If not: in the last four weeks, have you looked for work, and could you start? If yes, you're unemployed. If not, you're not in the labour force at all: retired, studying, caring for family, or simply not looking. The unemployment rate is the unemployed as a share of everyone working or looking. Whether you claim unemployment insurance plays no part.

On the Island, Dara runs the same survey, on all hundred adults. Here they are. Sixty-two worked last week, four of them part time though they wanted full time. Five looked for work and found none, two of them for more than fifteen weeks. Four more wanted work but weren't looking: two because they'd given up, two for other reasons. And twenty-nine didn't want a job: the old, the young in school, people caring for family. Sixty-two employed and five unemployed make a labour force of sixty-seven, and the unemployment rate is five out of sixty-seven: 7.5 percent.

But which people count as unemployed is a choice, so the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes six rates, from narrow to broad. Here they are for the Island. U-1 counts only the long-term unemployed: three percent. U-2, only people who lost a job. U-3 is the official rate, 7.5 percent. U-4 adds the discouraged, who want work but have given up looking. U-5 adds everyone else who wants a job and isn't looking. And U-6 adds the people working part time who want full time. On the Island it's 18.3 percent: same people, same week, and a rate more than twice as high.

In the United States, in October 2026, the six rates ran from 1.9 percent, for U-1, to 7.9 percent for U-6, with the official rate at 4.1. Since 1994, when the broad rates begin, U-3 and U-6 have moved together, the broad one roughly double the narrow one, both soaring in 2009 and in the spring of 2020. One more number keeps them honest: the share of adults in the labour force at all. It peaked at 67.3 percent in 2000 and is 61.9 now, partly because the population is older. The unemployment rate can fall because people find jobs, or because they stop looking.

A survey has to be taken to exist. Here is every month since January 1948, a square each: 946 of them, and every one has an unemployment rate, except one. In October 2025, during a shutdown of the federal government, the household survey wasn't carried out. There is no unemployment rate for that month, and there never will be. The number we treat as a fact of nature is the work of interviewers knocking on doors, and when they stop, it stops.
Distribution: Chapter nine. Who gets the income?

GDP per head is an average, and an average says nothing about how the income is shared. Kuznets warned about that too. Here are the Island's forty households, from poorest to richest, with what each received in the year: wages, profits and shares in the businesses. The average is 17 dollars 50. But two households stand far above it: Friday's, which owns the coconut grove, and Crusoe's, which owns the boatyard and half the fishing company. Between them they receive a quarter of all the income.

In 1905 an American student, Max Lorenz, found a picture for this. Line the households up from poorest to richest, and plot the share of all income received by the poorest ten percent, the poorest twenty, and so on. If everyone had the same income, the curve would be the diagonal. On the Island the poorer half of households receive 25 percent of the income, so the curve sags below it. In 1912 the Italian statistician Corrado Gini turned the sag into a number: the area between the diagonal and the curve, as a share of the whole triangle. Zero means everyone has the same; one means a single household has everything. The Island's Gini is 0.39; for wages alone, without the profits, it would be 0.26.

Here is the Gini index for 131 countries, each from its latest household survey, on a scale of nought to a hundred. The most equal, like Slovakia and Sweden, are in the twenties. Germany is in the thirties, China a little higher, the United States at 42, and the most unequal, Brazil, South Africa and their neighbours, in the fifties. A warning before comparing them: some countries survey income and others survey what households consume, which is more equal than income, because people borrow and save.

Surveys miss the very rich, who rarely answer them. So in the 2010s Thomas Piketty, Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman tried something new: take all of national income, the same total as the accounts, and split it among adults, using tax records for the top. In their estimates for the United States, the bottom half of adults received about 20 percent of pre-tax income in 1980 and 12 percent in 2014. The top one percent went the other way, from about 12 percent to 20. The two groups had swapped their shares. Their numbers were challenged. Gerald Auten and David Splinter, economists at the Treasury and at Congress's Joint Committee on Taxation, built the same kind of accounts with different assumptions about income that never shows up on tax returns, and found the top one percent's pre-tax share rising 4.4 points, about half as much, and only 1.4 after taxes and transfers. Both teams used the same national accounts. They disagree about the parts no record shows. Part 40 takes up the argument.
Leontief: Dara's books hold one more table, and it has its own history. In 1936 Wassily Leontief, an economist at Harvard who had left the Soviet Union in 1925, published a table of the American economy of 1919, showing what every industry bought from every other. Here is the Island's version. Each row is a seller, each column a buyer: the grove sold 20 dollars of fibre to the fishing company and 30 of coconut wood to the boatyard; the boatyard did 40 dollars of repairs for the fishers and 25 for the ferry. Divide each column by that business's total sales, and you get Leontief's coefficients: how much of each input it needs for every dollar it sells. Each dollar of fish needs about five cents of fibre, ten cents of repairs and four cents of freight. Leontief's bet was that these recipes stay roughly fixed, at least for a while.

Now ask the question Leontief built the table to answer. Suppose the visiting ships want ten dollars more fish. How much more must every business on the Island produce? First, ten dollars of fish. But catching it uses up fibre, repairs and freight, so the grove, the boatyard and the ferry must make about two dollars more between them. And those inputs need inputs of their own: the boatyard needs coconut wood, the ferry needs repairs. That's the second round, about thirty cents. Each round is smaller than the one before, and they add up. In all, the Island must produce 12.32 dollars more to deliver ten dollars of fish.

All the rounds at once is a matrix sum: the order, plus what the order needs, plus what that needs, and so on. Because each round shrinks, the sum converges, to a single matrix Leontief could compute directly: the inverse of the identity minus the coefficients. Each column says what every business must produce to deliver one more dollar of one product. Add up a column and you get that product's output multiplier: a dollar of fish needs 1.23 dollars of output in all, a dollar of passages on the ferry 1.27. The same arithmetic answered how much steel and rubber a fleet of ships would need in the Second World War, and won Leontief the Nobel prize in 1973.

The inverse also answers a question about trade. The Island exports 120 dollars of fish and coconuts. But how much of that was made on the Island? Trace every export back through all its rounds of inputs, and keep only the value added at home along the way: 111 dollars, 92 percent. The rest is the imported nets, nails and fuel buried inside the fish. For the world this matters a great deal. A phone assembled in one country counts in the trade statistics as that country's export, though its parts were made in many others. Since 2013 the OECD and the World Trade Organization have published trade measured by value added, using Leontief's method on tables of the whole world. We'll use them in Part 36.
Revisions: Chapter eleven. Revisions: the recession nobody saw at first.

Every number in this part is an estimate, and estimates are revised. The Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia keeps every version of America's GDP as it was first published and as it was revised, quarter by quarter, since 1965. Here is real GDP growth in 2008, as it stood in August of that year: a slowdown, nothing worse. By November, the third quarter showed a small fall. On the first of December 2008, the committee that dates American recessions announced that one had begun a year before, in December 2007. The numbers then published barely showed it. In February 2009 the first estimate for the fourth quarter arrived: a fall of 3.8 percent at an annual rate. Then the revisions came. The first quarter of 2008 turned from growth to decline. The fourth quarter was revised down, and down again, and it now stands at an annualized fall of 8.5 percent: more than twice as deep as first reported. The recession everyone lived through was worse than the numbers said at the time, and policy was made on those numbers.

Was 2008 unusual? Here is every quarter from 1965 to 2023: the growth first published, across, against the growth we believe today, up. If first estimates were final, every dot would sit on the dashed line. They scatter around it. The typical revision is 1.5 percentage points of annualized growth, when growth itself averages about three, and revisions have more often been upward. In 17 quarters, the first estimate didn't even get the sign right: growth became decline, or decline growth. Still, the first numbers carry most of the signal: they correlate 0.89 with today's.

Why revise? Because the first estimate is a race. The advance estimate comes about a month after a quarter ends, when much of the data hasn't arrived and the rest is projected from trends. It's revised in each of the next two months, then once a year, as tax records and annual surveys of businesses arrive, and every five years or so in a comprehensive revision, which can change the definitions themselves. In 2013 the Bureau of Economic Analysis began counting research and development as investment, and rewrote GDP all the way back to 1929. Central banks and governments can't wait for the final numbers, so they act on the first ones. Part 31 shows what that did to policy in the 1970s.
Beyond: By 1970 many people wondered whether growth of GDP was worth having at all. In 1972 William Nordhaus and James Tobin answered with the accounts themselves. They built a measure of economic welfare: GDP, plus the value of leisure and of work done at home, plus the services people get from the cars and houses and machines they own; minus what they called regrettables, spending like defence and commuting that is a cost of living rather than a benefit, minus the disamenities of crowded cities. From 1929 to 1965, they found, welfare per head grew 1.1 percent a year, against 1.7 for net national product. Slower, but growing. Their title asked whether growth was obsolete, and their answer was no.

The best-known alternative is the Human Development Index, published by the United Nations since 1990 and designed by the economist Mahbub ul Haq with Amartya Sen. It averages three things: how long people live, how much schooling they get, and their income, counted on a log scale so that an extra dollar matters less to the rich. Here it is for 193 countries, against income per head. It's tightly tied to income: the correlation with log income is 0.96, partly because income is one of its three parts. The interesting countries are the ones off the line: some, like Cuba and Tonga, do far better at keeping people alive and in school than their income alone would suggest, and others far worse, among them several rich in oil and gas, like Qatar, Brunei and Guyana, where income has outrun health and schooling.

The most economic answer came in 2016, from Charles Jones and Peter Klenow. They asked a single question: what share of an American's consumption would make you indifferent between living in America and living in another country, given each country's consumption, leisure, life expectancy and inequality? Here are their thirteen countries, around 2005: income per person in gold, their welfare measure in green, the United States set at a hundred. France has 67 percent of America's income and 60 percent of its consumption. But the French live about three years longer, work far fewer hours, and share consumption more equally. Counting those, French welfare is 92 percent of America's. For the poorer countries it goes the other way: shorter lives and more inequality put welfare below income. Across countries the two measures correlate at 0.98, so GDP per head is a good first guide. But the typical gap between them is about a third, and gaps like that are exactly what Kuznets warned about in 1934.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: how biased is the price index?

This part enters a new dial: how far the consumer price index overstates the rise in the cost of living, in percentage points a year. Its estimates come from expert reviews, which add up the bias source by source from many smaller studies. The Boskin Commission put it at 1.1 points for the mid-1990s, plausibly from 0.8 to 1.6. After the bureau's reforms, David Lebow and Jeremy Rudd put it at 0.87, with a plausible range from 0.3 to 1.4. Robert Gordon, one of the original commissioners, looked back in 2006: with what was known by then, the 1990s bias had been more like 1.2 or 1.3, and the bias of 2006 about 0.8. And Brent Moulton's audit for 2017 found 0.85. The status is settled within a range: the index overstates inflation, by somewhere between a few tenths of a point and a point and a half a year, and the best single guess has stayed close to one. Over a decade that compounds, and every indexed payment drifts with it.

The sources tell you what the reforms fixed. In 1996: a quarter of a point from substitution within goods, six tenths from new products and quality, and the rest from switching between goods and between shops. By 2003 the geometric means had cut the bias within goods to a twentieth of a point, and better quality adjustment had cut the largest part by about a third. But the chained index revealed more substitution between goods than the commission had thought. Moulton's update keeps the same shape. What remains is mostly Bo's problem, switching between goods, which a fixed basket can't see, and the hardest problem of all: putting a price on things that are new.

The accounts also produced the first facts of growth. In 1961 Nicholas Kaldor listed six that a theory of growth would have to explain, every one of them a reading of the national accounts. The first is in the data: American output per head, on a log scale, has grown along a nearly straight line since 1870, about 1.7 percent a year, through depressions and wars. The fifth has held less well. The share of income paid to labour stayed near 63 percent for decades and has fallen since 2000, to 57 percent by 2023. These facts are entered on the series' list here. Part 20 builds the model that explains Kaldor's facts, and Part 39 asks why labour's share fell.
